Wow!

One of the classic Scottish pipe tunes, and I love to hear it played by proficient pipers or fiddlers.

I tried to learn it several times by myself but cannot imitate that impulsive drive. Are there any good tips to play this kind of bouncy strathspeys?

↳ Posted by Jamie on June 15th, 2003.

It’s quite common to see this in a reel version as well, and moving from s to r is quite a common (many would say overdone) trick.

↳ Posted by Calum on May 29th, 2004.

For Slainte, a tip for getting a drive into your strathspeys is to tap your foot on every beat rather then every second beat. This tip comes courtesy of Wendy MacIsaac, a great CB fiddler. I was in a workshop with her and she said that doing this will help you to accent every beat. And another tip is to physically lift your bow off the strings where it permits. Hope this helps!

The Devil In The Kitchen

This is NOT by Scott Skinner, but he arranged it and published it in one of his books. It was composed by a piper, William Ross, and has the alternative name of “The Prince of Wales Jig”.

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on December 19th, 2005.

Another recording

In addition to the recordings listed, Dave Swarbrick & Simon Nicol recorded this on “Live at the White Bear” (1981) (since re-released as the compilation “Close to the White Bear” 1998).

Swarb also recorded it as a member of Fairport Convention on “Live Convention” (1974).

In both cases it is twinned with The Jolly Tinker under the name “Fiddlestix”.

On the Fairport recording the medley is attributed to “Pipe Major W. Ross” in addition to the players, though it’s not clear which of the two tunes is by Ross.

“Devil in the Kitchen Highland Fling”

I’ve known this as a highland fling played in the North, Donegal and elsewhere. I’d also come across it down South too. It is a favourite, a great tune and there are a lot of ways with it and it is played in several keys.

Here follows a version rescued from the future, suspecting impending doom for the contribution as it is not significantly different:

↳ Posted by Aaron Bergen on December 3rd, 2023.

Re: The Devil In The Kitchen

Simple chords are good, Aaron, it’s just that most people would hear the first chord as A rather than D given that A is the root. Is the D a modern thing?

↳ Posted by DonaldK on December 4th, 2023.

Re: The Devil In The Kitchen

Not really, A is the fifth of the D Major chord so having a melody note within that chord can happen, it’s just not as harmonious as playing a root melody note of D on a D major, or A on an A major. Also, with the A mixolydian mode holding the F# and C#, the same as D major, I think it’s really just a matter of preference. If I was putting together a performance piece, I possibly would have used different chord. I played those next to a chord player and it sounded just fine, and especially at tempo, it is less noticeable.

Personally, I also like adding a bit of harmony tension to some tunes as well and set them with another tune that jives a little easier. I think it can add a bit of spice to a set. In my opinion of course, as with so much in music, it’s personal preference

↳ Posted by Aaron Bergen on December 5th, 2023.

Re: The Devil In The Kitchen

Indeed, but I would have thought if one were adding “very basic chording” one would stick to the obvious chords.

It can be fun to start on the IV chord in a mixolydian or dorian tune (as, say, Session A9 do on Aird Ranters) but I wouldn’t use that if I wanted to demonstrate “very basic chording”.

Personally, I would always start with the obvious chords and work from there, although I do realise that for some people the “obvious” chords maybe aren’t so obvious (judging by what I see and hear).

Re: The Devil In The Kitchen

This tune (transposed to b flat) was used as one of the bagpipe sections of David Soldier’s “Most Unwanted Song” project.

I wouldn’t add it as a proper recording, but definitely seek it out if you want to be bewildered for 20 minutes.
